Intonation in Lists, Choice Questions and Non-Final Thought Groups

Intonation is the rise and fall of your voice. There are definite and expected intonation patterns in English.  The more you practice listening to and saying the correct intonation patterns, the better you will understand and be understood.

When naming items in a list, you use rising intonation for the first item in the list and falling intonation for the last. Falling intonation indicates the end of the list.

For example:

I like bananas ⤴, apples ⤴, pears ⤴ and grapes ⤵.

The rising intonation indicates to the listener that you are not finished and that there are other items in the list.

All choice questions have an 'or' in them and can either be an open or closed question. Open and closed choice questions have different intonation patterns and require a different kind of answer.

An open choice question is a kind of yes or no question. It has two possible intonation patterns.
For example:
Does she like Batman ↗or Superman ↗?
Does she like Batman or Superman ↗?

In this case, the possible answers could be yes or no answers:
Yes, she likes Batman .
Yes, she likes both.
No, she doesn't like either.
No, she doesn't like Batman but she likes Spiderman.

A closed choice question has limited choices. It cannot be answered by yes or no answers, and implies a choice between one option or the other.

For example:
Does she like Batman ↗ or Superman↘?

In the case, the possible answers could be:
She likes Batman.
She likes Superman.
She likes both.

A thought group refers to a coherent unit of speech that forms a whole. You normally separate a long sentence into several thought groups. Non-final thought groups represent all the thought groups that you say before the last thought group of a sentence. The final thought group is the thought group that ends a sentence.
You stress non-final thought groups with a normal-rising-normal pattern.

For example:
It's something I always did, … an aspect of who I am. A combination of things made me decide to write, … but losing my job when my son was born was a major factor.

Read the following sentences, keeping in mind the different intonation patterns you use:
Every author I read inspires me to improve, develop, and evolve as a writer.
What or who inspires or influences your writing?
The number one thing I'd do differently is to focus more on my strengths as a writer, … and focus more energy on writing, not revising.
How to Master an Interview
When you attend an interview, there are certain things that you can do to master it.

1. Get ready for the big day
Research the author, type up some ideas to bring up, think about answers to common interview questions (Tell me about yourself, Why do you want this job? etc.), Prepare your own questions, Put together an interview kit (pens, notepad, tissues, breath mints etc.)

2. Be your most authentic professional self
Be aware of your body language and eye contact. Try to relax and show your personality.

3. Follow other interview dos and don'ts
Arrive early, remember the name of the person you're interviewing, give them time to think of answers, send a thank-you note after the interview.
Choose a person you know that you would like to know more about.
Write down 10 questions you would ask this person about their professional experiences.
Contact this person and set up an appointment with them.
Ask them your questions and write down their answers.
Remember to thank them for their time.

Kristi: Thanks for taking the time to sit down with me.
Mr. Duncan: Not a problem.
Kristi: What made you decide to become a writer?
Mr. Duncan: I didn't exactly decide to become a writer. It's something I always did, an aspect of who I am. A combination of things made me decide to write, but losing my job when my son was born was a major factor. It was the perfect time to recommit myself to writing.
Kristi: How long did it take to get published the first time and how did it happen?
Mr. Duncan: At one time or another, I tried my hand at everything from poetry to children's picture books, comedy sketches and teleplays. I pitched to an editor in the spring of 2006, followed up on the submission in early 2007, and was picked up by the publisher a few weeks later.

Kristi: What would you do differently the next time?
Mr. Duncan: What would I do differently? How long do you have? The number one thing I'd do differently is to focus more on my strengths as a writer, and focus more energy on writing, not revising.
Kristi: What advice would you give an aspiring author?
Mr. Duncan: Identify your strengths, make that your mantra, and then persist!
Kristi: What or who inspires or influences your writing?
Mr. Duncan: Every author I read inspires me to improve, develop, and evolve as a writer.

Kristi: How long have you been writing professionally?
Mr. Duncan: On and off, for about 30 years.
Kristi: What do you do for fun when you are not writing?
Mr. Duncan: I might walk on the beach, do some gardening, read and spend time with family.
Kristi: I think that's it. Thanks again, Mr. Duncan. I appreciate you taking the time to answer my questions.
